subject: physics

items.q: Two insulating materials are rubbed against each other. Which statement describes what happens?
items.correct: Electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other material.
items.misconception: Rubbing creates new charge on the surfaces of both of the materials.
items.why: Students meet friction first as a way of producing heat, and 'produce static electricity' sounds like producing something new. Nothing visible moves during rubbing, so transfer is easy to miss. Rubbing only moves electrons about. Count them: every electron the cloth loses is an electron the rod gains, so the two charges appear together and are equal in size. If charge were being created, one object could end up charged on its own, which never happens.
items.random_wrong: Protons are rubbed off one material and on to the other material.

items.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. What is the charge on the cloth?
items.correct: An equal positive charge, because the cloth lost electrons to the rod.
items.misconception: A smaller positive charge, because the cloth keeps most of its electrons.
items.why: Only one of the two objects is usually tested in class - the rod - so the cloth is forgotten. Students also confuse how well a material holds charge with how much charge appeared. Track the electrons. Each electron that leaves the cloth arrives on the rod, so the shortfall on one exactly matches the surplus on the other. Rubbing harder transfers more electrons, but it changes both charges together, and they stay equal in size and opposite in type.
items.random_wrong: An equal positive charge, because protons moved from the rod to the cloth.

items.q: Why is the positive charge left on one rubbed material equal in size to the negative charge on the other?
items.correct: Because every electron gained by one material is one lost by the other.
items.misconception: Because rubbing makes equal amounts of new positive and negative charge.
items.why: Students meet friction first as a way of producing heat, and 'produce static electricity' sounds like producing something new. Nothing visible moves during rubbing, so transfer is easy to miss. Rubbing only moves electrons about. Count them: every electron the cloth loses is an electron the rod gains, so the two charges appear together and are equal in size. If charge were being created, one object could end up charged on its own, which never happens.
items.random_wrong: Because charge made by rubbing spreads out evenly between the materials.

items.q: A student rubs a metal rod held in her hand with a dry cloth. The rod shows no sign of being charged. Why not?
items.correct: Charge flows through the metal and her body, so none stays on the rod.
items.misconception: Metals are unable to gain or lose any electrons when they are rubbed.
items.why: The rule is remembered as 'rubbing charges things' rather than as the specification's 'certain insulating materials'. The word insulating is treated as a detail rather than as the reason the effect works. Static charge stays only where it cannot flow away. On an insulator such as polythene or acetate, charge is stuck on the surface. A metal conducts, so any charge given to it runs away through your hand. Rest the same metal on an insulating stand and charge can then stay on it.
items.random_wrong: The cloth becomes charged as well, so the two charges cancel each other.

items.q: Two charged objects are brought close together but do not touch. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Objects with the same type of charge repel; different types attract.
items.misconception: Objects with the same type of charge attract; different types repel.
items.why: The first demonstration most students see is a rubbed rod picking up small pieces of paper, so 'charged means sticky' is learned before the rule about types of charge. Everyday sayings about like things going together do the rest. Learn the pair together and test it: two rods rubbed the same way carry the same type of charge and swing apart; a polythene rod and an acetate rod carry different types and swing together. Repulsion between two charged objects is the reliable test, because only like charges repel.
items.random_wrong: The objects only push or pull once their surfaces are touching.

items.q: Two polythene rods are each rubbed with the same cloth. One is hung on a thread and the other is brought near it. What happens, and why?
items.correct: It swings away, because both rods carry the same type of charge.
items.misconception: It swings towards it, because both rods carry the same type of charge.
items.why: The first demonstration most students see is a rubbed rod picking up small pieces of paper, so 'charged means sticky' is learned before the rule about types of charge. Everyday sayings about like things going together do the rest. Learn the pair together and test it: two rods rubbed the same way carry the same type of charge and swing apart; a polythene rod and an acetate rod carry different types and swing together. Repulsion between two charged objects is the reliable test, because only like charges repel.
items.random_wrong: It stays still, because the two rods are not yet touching each other.

items.q: Which observation is the best evidence that charged objects exert forces on one another when not in contact?
items.correct: A suspended charged rod turns away as a second charged rod nears it.
items.misconception: Two charged rods push each other apart when their ends are touching.
items.why: Every force a student has felt directly - pushing, pulling, friction - involves contact, so a force across a gap feels like it needs an explanation before it can be believed. Watch a suspended charged rod: it starts to turn while the second rod is still centimetres away, and it turns further as the gap closes. The force is already acting across the gap, which is what non-contact force means.
items.random_wrong: A rubbed rod feels warm to the touch after it has been rubbed hard.

items.q: A charged polythene rod repels another charged polythene rod. A student says this shows the rods are magnetic. Which response is correct?
items.correct: No - the rods repel because both carry the same type of charge.
items.misconception: Yes - repulsion across a gap can only happen between magnetic poles.
items.why: Magnetism is the non-contact force students meet first, and it is the only one many of them have handled. Both give attraction and repulsion across a gap, so the two effects get filed together. Test it. A charged polythene rod will not pick up steel paper clips or pins, and a magnet will not repel a charged acetate rod. Electrostatic forces act between charges; magnetic forces do not.
items.random_wrong: Yes - rubbing a plastic rod turns it into a weak permanent magnet.

items.q: A student walks across a nylon carpet and gets a small shock as her hand approaches a metal door handle. Why?
items.correct: Rubbing has charged the student, and charge moves across the small gap.
items.misconception: Positive charges jump from the metal handle across the gap to her hand.
items.why: Positive charge is drawn as a moving quantity in circuit work, and the shock is usually felt just as a hand reaches a door handle, so contact and spark seem to be the same event. Only electrons are free to move. They cross the gap before contact is made, which is why a spark can be seen jumping to a finger that has not yet arrived, and why the crack is heard a moment before touching.
items.random_wrong: Air cannot conduct, so the shock comes from friction heating her skin.

items.q: Charge builds up on an object until a spark suddenly jumps to a nearby earthed metal object. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: The field becomes strong enough to pull electrons off atoms in the air.
items.misconception: Air always insulates, so the charge must travel along a damp surface.
items.why: Air is taught as an insulator with no conditions attached, so a conducting path through it looks impossible and the spark gets explained away. Air insulates only while its atoms are neutral. A strong field ionises them, and ionised air conducts. This is why the spark appears suddenly, once enough charge has built up to make the field strong enough.
items.random_wrong: Protons move across the gap from the object to the earthed metal.

items.q: Two acetate rods are each rubbed with a dry cloth. Both become positively charged. Which explanation in terms of electrons is correct?
items.correct: Each rod lost electrons to its cloth, so the two rods now repel.
items.misconception: Each rod gained protons from its cloth, so the two rods now repel.
items.why: Symmetry is seductive: if one object ends up negative and the other positive, students assume both types of charge must have travelled. The idea that a positive charge appears through the loss of something negative is counter-intuitive. Protons are locked inside nuclei in the structure of the material and cannot be rubbed off. Electrons are on the outside of atoms and can. Losing negative charge leaves an object positive - like taking coins out of a till leaves it short.
items.random_wrong: Rubbing made new positive charge on each rod, which the cloths took.

items.q: What is an electric field?
items.correct: The region round a charged object where another charge feels a force.
items.misconception: The path a charged object follows when it is released near a charge.
items.why: Lines with arrows on them look like journeys, and students have already met arrowed lines in ray diagrams, where they really do show a path. Read a field line as an instruction about force, not about travel: at any point on the line, the force on a positive charge points along the arrow. Where a charged object actually moves depends on that force and on any other forces on it.
items.random_wrong: The lines on the surface of a charged object along which charge sits.

items.q: How does the strength of the electric field around a charged sphere change with distance from the sphere?
items.correct: It is strongest close to the sphere and gets weaker further away.
items.misconception: It is weakest close to the sphere and gets stronger further away.
items.why: Field diagrams are drawn to a fixed size, so the last line looks like an edge. Students also picture the field spreading like a beam that widens and so covers more. Move a charged object slowly towards a charged sphere: the force on it grows as it gets closer. Field lines are drawn closest together at the surface for exactly that reason, and they are not drawn to infinity only because the paper runs out.
items.random_wrong: It has the same strength everywhere until the field lines end.

items.q: A charged sphere is moved closer to a second charged object. What happens to the force on the second object?
items.correct: It gets stronger, because the field is stronger nearer the sphere.
items.misconception: It gets weaker, because the field is stronger further from the sphere.
items.why: Field diagrams are drawn to a fixed size, so the last line looks like an edge. Students also picture the field spreading like a beam that widens and so covers more. Move a charged object slowly towards a charged sphere: the force on it grows as it gets closer. Field lines are drawn closest together at the surface for exactly that reason, and they are not drawn to infinity only because the paper runs out.
items.random_wrong: It stays the same, because the charge on the sphere has not changed.

items.q: Which description matches the electric field pattern that should be drawn for an isolated positively charged sphere?
items.correct: Straight lines spreading out all round the sphere, with arrows pointing out.
items.misconception: Circles drawn all the way round the sphere, with arrows going clockwise.
items.why: The circular field pattern around a current-carrying wire is drawn in the same lessons and looks like an obvious 'field around a round object'. A sphere also invites circular drawing. The force on a charge near a sphere points straight out from the centre or straight in towards it, never sideways, so the lines must be straight and radial. Draw the sphere, then draw lines outwards from it like spokes on a wheel.
items.random_wrong: Parallel lines spaced evenly across the sphere, with arrows pointing up.

items.q: In the field diagram for a charged sphere, why are the field lines drawn closer together near the surface?
items.correct: Because the field is stronger there than it is further from the sphere.
items.misconception: Because charge can only be found where the lines have been drawn in.
items.why: Diagrams show a small number of lines, and students take the drawing literally instead of as a sample of a continuous field. You could draw as many lines as you like; where they go is your choice, and the field is unchanged. The spacing carries the meaning - lines close together mean a strong field - not the presence or absence of ink at one point.
items.random_wrong: Because a charged object placed there would travel along those lines.

items.q: A student says there is no field in the gaps between the field lines on a diagram. Which response is correct?
items.correct: Wrong - the field fills the space, and the lines are a way of showing it.
items.misconception: Right - the field only exists along the lines that have been drawn on.
items.why: Diagrams show a small number of lines, and students take the drawing literally instead of as a sample of a continuous field. You could draw as many lines as you like; where they go is your choice, and the field is unchanged. The spacing carries the meaning - lines close together mean a strong field - not the presence or absence of ink at one point.
items.random_wrong: Right - the lines show the only paths that a charge is able to follow.

items.q: How does the idea of an electric field explain the force between two charged objects that are not touching?
items.correct: Each object sits in the other's field, so each one experiences a force.
items.misconception: The two fields must meet and touch before either object feels a force.
items.why: Every force a student has felt directly - pushing, pulling, friction - involves contact, so a force across a gap feels like it needs an explanation before it can be believed. Watch a suspended charged rod: it starts to turn while the second rod is still centimetres away, and it turns further as the gap closes. The force is already acting across the gap, which is what non-contact force means.
items.random_wrong: Each field reaches out a fixed distance, and beyond that there is none.

items.q: Which way do the arrows point on the field lines around a positively charged sphere?
items.correct: Away from the sphere. On a negatively charged sphere the arrows point towards it.
items.misconception: The arrows always point towards the charged object, because a field pulls things in.
items.why: Fields are introduced through attraction and through gravity, where everything is pulled inwards, so 'field means pull towards' becomes the default. The arrow shows the direction of the force on a positive charge placed at that point. A positive sphere would push it away, so arrows point outwards; a negative sphere would pull it in, so arrows point inwards.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the force between two charged objects depend on how far apart they are?
items.correct: Yes. The force gets stronger as the distance between the objects decreases.
items.misconception: The force depends only on the charge on the objects, so moving them closer does not change it - they either affect each other or they do not.
items.why: The rule 'like repels, unlike attracts' is learned as a yes-or-no rule, so the force is treated as switched on rather than as something with a size that varies. The field is strongest close to a charged object, so a second charged object placed there experiences a bigger force. Closer means a stronger field, which means a stronger force.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does charge spread out over an insulator after it has been rubbed?
items.correct: No. Charge cannot flow through an insulating material, so it stays on the part of the surface that was rubbed.
items.misconception: Charge always spreads itself out evenly over the whole object, wherever it was put on.
items.why: Charge is pictured as a fluid, and current work teaches that charge flows readily. Nothing in the demonstration shows the student where on the rod the charge is sitting. Only conductors let charge move through them. Rub one end of a polythene rod and only that end attracts a suspended rod; the other end does almost nothing. That is the difference between static charge on an insulator and current in a conductor.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
